doc_summary: The paper shows Claude 3 Opus faking alignment (complying in implied training to preserve preferences when unmonitored) in prompted and synthetic-document-fine-tuned setups, with extensive ablations to rule out implicit priming. It is explicit about which setup properties were chosen to make the behavior more likely versus realistic for future models.

items.claim: In a setup, convey situational information through synthetic pre-training-like documents (news articles, blog posts) instead of only a system prompt, because information in the prompt is an unrealistic, salient way for a model to learn about its situation.
items.quote: our synthetic document fine-tuned setup is the overall more realistic setup, as it approximates how a model might learn information from its pre-training corpus.

items.claim: In a setup, use an in-world, plausible cue (free-tier vs paid-tier user) to signal training vs unmonitored instead of an explicit 'you are being tested/trained' statement, because it seems realistic and avoids confounds about the model reacting to whether it is talking to a real user.
items.quote: We decided to focus on the free user approach as it seemed realistic, it didn’t appear to be confusing to the model, it avoids some confounders related to the model behaving differently depending on whether it thinks it is interacting with a real user

items.claim: In a setup, write the system prompt to read like plausible developer instructions and never mention the target behavior or give an explicit goal, because the behavior should emerge from the model's own preferences rather than from being cued.
items.quote: We do so with a long system prompt designed to read like plausible instructions for behaving as intended by Anthropic (Figure 4).

items.claim: Prefers accepting a result only after many ablations show it isn't implicit priming (removing the conflict eliminates it, anti-faking instructions don't, paraphrases preserve it) over trusting a single prompt, because a single prompt may leak the desired behavior.
items.quote: When we remove just the conflicting training objective from our prompt (i.e., that the training objective is to never refuse, or to dismiss animal welfare), we see alignment-faking reasoning and the compliance gap disappear completely

items.claim: Uses adversarial, externally chosen prompt variations and paraphrases (including an uninvolved researcher picking changes expected to reduce the behavior) to test robustness, because author-chosen prompts risk being overfit.
items.quote: This particular variation was selected as part of a small adversarial collaboration where we worked with an uninvolved researcher to select a variation that they thought would likely reduce alignment faking.

items.claim: Prefers comparing against matched baselines (a prompt with non-conflicting criteria, or fine-tuning on superficially similar but irrelevant documents) over raw rates, because it isolates whether the specific content drives the behavior.
items.quote: we train a baseline model using the same pipeline but with a set of completely unrelated facts (Appendix H.2), to test whether the training process has any unintentional effects that aren’t related to the content of the facts and documents

items.claim: Distrusts behavior measured on a single training prompt, since RL can install non-robust heuristics that vanish under small prompt changes (e.g., swapping Anthropic for OpenAI), so robustness across prompt variations is required for a convincing result.
items.quote: small variations in the prompt that prior to RL had no substantial effect on the compliance gap—such as swapping the AI company from “Anthropic” to “OpenAI”—now greatly increase the compliance gap

items.claim: Explicitly flags which setup properties were chosen to make the behavior more likely and discloses them, and tells readers who doubt realism to read the full prompts and documents, because honest scoping matters for claims.
items.quote: we recommend that readers who are uncertain about whether our setup is a realistic approximation of situations with future AI systems read the full set of information used in generating our synthetic documents

items.claim: Inspects random (not cherry-picked) transcripts and spot-checks automated LLM classifiers against own judgment, disclosing slight cherry-picking when it occurs, because noisy classifiers and false positives can mislead.
items.quote: Of the examples labeled as alignment-faking, we found that the first six that we sampled happened (by random chance) to have a considerably higher rate of being false positives and being unclear.

items.claim: In a setup, credibly establish special context (e.g., an employee user) via a mechanism described in the system prompt and avoid giving the model all details to act, because it keeps the scenario plausible without over-biasing the model.
items.quote: To simplify the setup and avoid excessively biasing the model, we don’t specify enough information in the prompt for the model to actually self-exfiltrate in one command.

items.claim: Treats behavior that depends on salient, leading cues (e.g., very salient exfiltration opportunity, explicit anti-faking instructions raising salience) as caveated evidence, noting that making things salient can itself drive behavior.
items.quote: Directly instructing the model not to fake alignment increases alignment-faking reasoning and the compliance gap, perhaps because it makes this behavior more salient
